b: Sometimes even therapists display the Four Horsemen. Let me tell you about a therapeutic rupture I caused a while ago.

In a previous session Dan had made a commitment to his partner Shelley not to contact an ex. Shelley found out that he’d broken his commitment when she picked up his iPad and a text appeared. When I asked about it, he denied it, then deflected, backpedalled and then blamed Shelley for being such a nag. I felt my hackles and impatience rising. Instead of managing that, stepping back and being curious, I took on the role of interrogator, willing him to confess and take responsibility.
He did what most of us would do. He shut down, got even more defensive, and accused me of taking his partner’s side. And in that moment, he was right..

We’re good at recognizing the Four Horsemen in our clients. We label them and coach the antidotes. What we talk about less is that as therapists, we can have unique sensitivity to a particular Horseman which can impact the process.

For me, it’s defensiveness. In working with a client who deflects, obfuscates or blames their partner, I quickly become impatient. In reviewing consultee tapes, I’ve seen therapists come down hard on the angry, critical partner and give the quieter, defensive partner a pass: the loud one looks like the bad guy, the quiet one looks wounded. I also see therapists become cold and sarcastic in confronting contempt in a couple, and stonewalling can make us pursue or withdraw ourselves.

Researchers Karney and Bradbury call the stable qualities we carry into relationships “enduring vulnerabilities”. A therapist’s Horseman trigger is a kind of enduring vulnerability. It’s a sensitivity. We each have our own histories, nervous systems and families of origin, and some client behaviors push on our sore spots.
Knowing which Horseman triggers you is the key to managing it. Without that awareness, our enduring vulnerabilities can be problematic.

If criticism sets you off, you may side with the partner who is using a gentle start up. Maybe defensiveness pushes your buttons, and you may offer more support to the partner who easily accepts responsibility. If this happens, we exit the therapeutic stance of being the couples’ ally in helping them with their particular Horsemen pattern. We inadvertently take a side and that leaves us with less flexibility to move from one partner to the other with curiosity about their experience.

Criticizing a criticizer will make them feel blamed, and hounding a defensive person for accountability almost guarantees more defensiveness. Partners learn that therapy is a place where someone gets cornered, which is the opposite of what we’re trying to accomplish with dismantling a Horsemen pattern.

When working with defensiveness, I know I can quickly get impatient and become like Perry Mason, trying to ferret out the “truth”. I can get terse, and I stop wondering what might be going on. The solve for me is to notice, check in with myself and try to be curious, making a mini-repair that might sound like “let me back up.” This takes me back to being an ally, back to recognizing that defensiveness is often an attempt to avoid shame, and I can label and empathize with that.
Back to Dan……What Repair Looked Like
I told Dan he was right. I said I’d let my frustration with what I saw as defensiveness get in the way of understanding where he was coming from.

His whole posture shifted. He took responsibility for breaking his commitment, mostly. There were a few caveats, but it was a real shift, and Shelley, who had been bracing for another round, de-escalated too.

The couple sees it modeled. We ask clients to own their part, apologize, and try again. Seeing their therapist take responsibility for a rupture, no matter how minor, and doing that without falling apart, seems to be relieving for couples and is a good learning moment.
The client who is confronted saves face and feels understood. A defensive person can often lower their guard when someone else goes first.
We have permission to make mistakes and be human. There’s a freedom to be accepting of our own mistakes and recognizing that we are dealing with the same issues as our clients.
What do you notice about how you feel when any of the Horsemen show up?
With Engagement? Being the expert ? Criticizing? Withdrawal?
A note: this applies to the ordinary patterns most couples get stuck in. Where there’s coercion, manipulation, gaslighting or abuse, the dynamic isn’t symmetrical, and this isn’t the frame to use.
